reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an Ethereum MEV trading bot as an easy passive-income opportunity while advertising returns of over $1,000 per day. It instructs viewers to deploy or fund the bot contract with at least 0.2 ETH, start it, and rely on the claimed ability to withdraw profits. The promotion also claims rapid and unusually high returns, including 31% after about 12 hours and prior gains of 3-6 ETH or more, although the speaker notes that profits fluctuate and the actual contract behavior is not established.

citations.quote: Make $1,000+/DAY with Ethereum MEV Trading Bot
Today I'll be teaching you step by step how to deploy an Ethereum trading bot
This sandwiches the target transactions and forces ours to be processed first, profiting off of the difference in slippage.
Deposit funds (at least .2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
We need to confirm the contract on the blockchain by paying gas fees.

opening.argument: Judge the income claim alongside the speaker's qualifications. The speaker says profits vary from week to week, and the description warns that insufficient funding can be consumed by gas fees when a token has high burn fees. Those are material limits on the advertised outcome, not a promise that every viewer will earn the headline amount. The discussion of funding is framed around trading costs and possible losses.

citations.quote: The profits will fluctuate week to week.
If you fund the contract with less than 0.2 ETH and the bot targets another token with high burn fees, the contract will waste a lot on gas fees.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The headline and reported 31% gain are striking, but neither establishes a guaranteed return for viewers. The funding threshold is explained in terms of costs, while the speaker explicitly acknowledges variable profits. A claim that the contract's actual behavior is unestablished is a reason to withhold certainty about its performance, not proof that the speaker intends to deceive.

citations.quote: Funding the contract with at least 0.2 ETH will ensure this won't happen.
The profits will fluctuate week to week.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The qualifications do not undo the central pitch. The title advertises daily income, and the instructions tell viewers to deposit at least 0.2 ETH into a contract. Warning that a smaller deposit could be lost to fees makes the funding instruction more forceful; it does not establish that the bot performs the promised trades or that withdrawals will work.

citations.quote: Make $1,000+/DAY with Ethereum MEV Trading Bot
Deposit funds (at least .2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address

opening.argument: The video is structured as a technical walkthrough. It tells viewers to create a Solidity file, paste the linked source code, choose a compiler version, and deploy through an injected provider. The speaker also describes checking addresses on Etherscan. That sequence gives the audience concrete operations to examine, rather than merely directing them to a hosted investment offer. The reported earnings are presented within a demonstration of the workflow; their accuracy should be assessed separately from whether the walkthrough itself is an attempt to deceive.

citations.quote: Right click the 'contracts' folder and create a new file called 'Bot.sol' :backhand index pointing right: Paste THIS code into Remix:
Move to the 'Solidity Compiler' tab, select version '0.6.6', then click 'Compile'
Lines 50 and 51, you can follow these addresses using etherscan.
as you can see I have about 1.31 Ethereum which is 31% profit already

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening accurately identifies the funding and profit claims, but those appear inside a step-by-step deployment demonstration. The speaker even directs viewers to check the contract address on Etherscan. That check does not verify the bot's trading behavior, but the absence of such verification also does not, by itself, turn every technical step into evidence of a scam.

citations.quote: So let's copy the smart contract address to make sure it's created. I'm going to head back over to etherscan and paste it in.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Technical steps do not make the video neutral education. The same instructions direct viewers to fund the contract and start it, while the speaker connects larger deposits to greater profits. Checking that an address exists cannot establish the asserted trading mechanism or the claimed returns.

citations.quote: Deposit funds (at least .2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
the more. You put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich and the more profit. You will be able to accumulate over time.

opening.argument: The described transaction is deployment of a contract through the viewer's wallet, with network gas fees, rather than a stated purchase of returns from the presenter. The instructions call the deployed contract the viewer's own bot and identify a withdrawal action. Those claims need verification, but the supplied account does not establish that the presenter receives the deposited ETH or asks for wallet credentials. The evidence supports scrutiny of the contract code and withdrawals; it does not identify a transfer to the presenter.

citations.quote: After the deployment transaction confirms, it's your own BOT now
We need to confirm the contract on the blockchain by paying gas fees. Gas fees are the commission on the Ethereum network for smart contract deployment.
Withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening establishes that viewers are told to fund a contract, but not who ultimately controls its funds. The quoted gas fee is described as a network deployment cost, not a payment to the presenter. Nor does an asserted 31% result establish an explicit guarantee to every viewer. Without verified contract behavior, the suspected diversion of deposits remains an inference.

citations.quote: Gas fees are the commission on the Ethereum network for smart contract deployment.
as you can see I have about 1.31 Ethereum which is 31% profit already

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A scam pitch need not request credentials or explicitly disclose where funds go. This one tells viewers to deposit ETH into a linked-code contract, activate it, and expect returns from purported sandwich trades. Calling it the viewer's own bot and describing a withdrawal button do not demonstrate control of the funds or prove the withdrawal claim.
